{{Short description|Product of any collection of compact topological spaces is compact}}
{{For|other theorems named after Tychonoff|Tychonoff's theorem (disambiguation)}}
{{CS1 config|mode=cs2}}
In [[mathematics]], '''Tychonoff's theorem''' states that the product of any collection of [[compact space|compact]] [[topological space]]s is compact with respect to the [[product topology]]. The theorem is named after [[Andrey Nikolayevich Tikhonov]] (whose surname sometimes is transcribed ''Tychonoff''), who proved it first in 1930 for powers of the closed [[unit interval]] and in 1935 stated the full theorem along with the remark that its proof was the same as for the special case. The earliest known published proof is contained in a 1935 article by Tychonoff, {{lang|de|italic=no|"Über einen Funktionenraum"}}.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Tikhonov |first=Andrey Nikolayevich |title=Über einen Funktionraum |language=de |journal=Mathematische Annalen |issue=111 |pages=762–766 |year=1935}}</ref>

Tychonoff's theorem is one of the most foundational results in general topology.<ref>{{cite book |last=Willard |first=Stephen |author-link=Stephen Willard |title=General Topology |year=2004 |publisher=Dover |isbn=978-0-486-43479-7 |page=120}}</ref> The theorem is also valid for topological spaces based on [[fuzzy sets]].<ref>{{cite journal |last=Goguen |first=Joseph |author-link=Joseph Goguen |title=The Fuzzy Tychonoff Theorem |journal=[[Journal of Mathematical Analysis and Applications]] |volume=43 |issue=3 |date=September 1973 |pages=734–742|doi=10.1016/0022-247X(73)90288-6 }}</ref>

== Statement ==
Here is the statement of the theorem.

{{math_theorem|name=Tychonoff's theorem|math_statement=Let <math>X_i, \, i \in I</math> be a family of compact spaces. Then their product
:<math>X := \prod_{i \in I} X_i</math>
is a compact space with respect to the [[product topology]] (meaning the [[initial topology]] with respect to the projections <math>p_i : X \to X_i</math>).}}

=== Strength ===
The above theorem turns out to be equivalent to the [[axiom of choice]]. There is a special case of the theorem saying
*A product of compact Hausdorff spaces <math>X_i</math> is compact Hausdorff. If, in addition, all the <math>X_i</math> are nonempty, then the product <math>\prod X_i</math> is nonempty.

This Hausdorff version of the theorem is actually strictly weaker than the axiom of choice and is equivalent to the [[Boolean prime ideal theorem]]. (Note for an arbitrary product, the axiom of choice ensures the product is nonempty when each factor is nonempty. But in the Hausdorff case, the above version can ensure the nonempty-ness without Choice. In fact, it implies a version of the axiom of choice; see {{section link||Application: the Hahn–Banach theorem}}.)

For a ''finite'' product of compact sets, the theorem is rather trivial (see {{section link||Tychonoff's theorem for finite products}} below) and does not depend on the axiom of choice or weaker variants.

== Tychonoff's theorem for finite products ==
For a finite product of compact spaces, the theorem is substantially easier. For example, it would follow from

<!-- the proof may be incomplete. see the talkpage 

''Proof'': We begin by proving that if <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math> are compact, then so is <math>X \times Y</math>. Let <math>\mathcal{U} = \{U_n\}</math> be an open cover of <math>X \times Y</math>, and let <math>p \colon X \times Y \to Y</math> be the projection map. For each <math>y \in Y</math>, the preimage <math>p^{-1}(y) \subseteq Y</math> is homeomorphic to <math>X</math> and therefore is compact, so we can find a finite subcollection <math>\mathcal{U}(y) = \{U_{n_1},\dots,U_{n_r}\}</math> which covers <math>p^{-1}(y)</math>. The projection <math> p \colon X \times Y \to Y</math> is an [[Open and closed maps#Open maps|open map]], so <math>p(U_{n_i})</math> is an open subset of <math>Y</math> for each <math>i</math>, and therefore the intersection <math>V(y) = \bigcap_{i=1}^r p(U_{n_i})</math> is an open subset of <math>Y</math> containing <math>y</math>. Repeating this for each <math>y \in Y</math>, we obtain an open cover of <math>Y</math> by the <math>V(y)</math>. Since <math>Y</math> is compact, this open cover has a finite subcover, which is to say we can choose <math>y_1,\dots,y_t</math> so that <math>V(y_1),\dots,V(y_t)</math> cover <math>Y</math>. Then the collection <math>\bigcup_{j=1}^t \mathcal{U}(y_j)</math> covers <math>X \times Y</math>, and is a finite union of finite sets, and is therefore finite.

The case for all finite products now follows by induction on the number of spaces in the product. <math>\square</math>

The above proof furthermore establishes that -->
*if <math>X</math> is a compact space and <math>Y</math> is any topological space, then the projection <math>p : X \times Y \to Y</math> is [[proper map|proper]]; i.e., the pre-image of a compact set is compact.<ref>Ch. I, § 8. Corollary 8.3., Bredon, G.E. (2013). Topology and Geometry. Graduate Texts in Mathematics. Vol. 139. Springer Science & Business Media.</ref>

Alternatively, the [[tube lemma]] can be used to give a direct proof; see {{section link|Tube lemma#Examples and properties}}.

=== Further remark ===
For a metric space, compactness is equivalent to [[sequentially compact space|sequential compactness]]. Using Cantor's diagonal argument, it is straightforward to show a countable product of sequentially compact spaces is sequentially compact space; thus, for metric spaces at least, this gives the theorem for a countable product.

However, for many applications, taking uncountable products is necessary. For example, taking <math>L = C(X, I)</math> to be the set of all continuous maps from a topological space <math>X</math> to the unit <math>I = [0, 1]</math>, we have the natural map
:<math>X \to \prod_L I, \, x \mapsto (f(x) \mid f).</math>
The closure of the image is exactly the [[Stone–Čech compactification]] <math>\beta X</math> of the space <math>X</math>;<ref>The natural map is an embedding if and only if <math>X</math> is a [[Tychonoff space]], but the construction here still goes through for arbitrary spaces.</ref> here, the compactness of <math>\beta X</math> is a consequence of Tychonoff's theorem.

== Applications ==

Tychonoff's theorem has been used to prove many other mathematical theorems. These include theorems about compactness of certain spaces such as the [[Banach–Alaoglu theorem]] on the weak-* compactness of the unit ball of the [[dual space]] of a [[normed vector space]], and the [[Arzelà–Ascoli theorem]] characterizing the sequences of functions in which every subsequence has a [[uniform convergence|uniformly convergent]] subsequence. They also include statements less obviously related to compactness, such as the [[De Bruijn–Erdős theorem (graph theory)|De Bruijn–Erdős theorem]] stating that every [[critical graph|minimal ''k''-chromatic graph]] is finite, and the [[Curtis–Hedlund–Lyndon theorem]] providing a topological characterization of [[cellular automaton|cellular automata]].

As a rule of thumb, any sort of construction that takes as input a fairly general object (often of an algebraic, or topological-algebraic nature) and outputs a compact space is likely to use Tychonoff: e.g., the [[Gelfand representation|Gelfand space]] of maximal ideals of a commutative [[C*-algebra]], the [[Stone space]] of maximal ideals of a [[Boolean algebra (structure)|Boolean algebra]], and the [[Berkovich spectrum]] of a commutative [[Banach ring]].

In logic, specifically [[model theory]], Tychonoff’s theorem implies the [[compactness theorem]], which says a theory (a set of sentences) has a model if and only if each finite subset of it does.

== Proofs ==

1) Tychonoff's 1930 proof used the concept of a [[complete accumulation point]].

2) The theorem is a quick corollary of the [[Alexander subbase theorem]].<ref>https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/08ZU {{Bare URL inline|date=September 2026}}</ref>
<!-- I get what this is trying to say, but it feels a bit unrelated to the theorem. Perhaps we should move it to [[filters in topology]]
More modern proofs have been motivated by the following considerations: the approach to compactness via convergence of subsequences leads to a simple and transparent proof in the case of countable index sets. However, the approach to convergence in a topological space using sequences is sufficient when the space satisfies the first axiom of countability (as metrizable spaces do), but generally not otherwise. However, the product of uncountably many metrizable spaces, each with at least two points, fails to be first countable. So it is natural to hope that a suitable notion of convergence in arbitrary spaces will lead to a compactness criterion generalizing sequential compactness in metrizable spaces that will be as easily applied to deduce the compactness of products. This has turned out to be the case.-->

3) The theory of convergence via [[filters in topology|filters]], due to [[Henri Cartan]] and developed by [[Nicolas Bourbaki|Bourbaki]], leads to the following criterion: assuming the [[ultrafilter lemma]], a space is compact if and only if each [[Ultrafilter (set theory)|ultrafilter]] on the space converges. With this in hand, the proof becomes easy: the (filter generated by the) image of an ultrafilter on the product space under any projection map is an ultrafilter on the factor space, which therefore converges, to at least one ''x<sub>i</sub>''. One then shows that the original ultrafilter converges to ''x''&nbsp;=&nbsp;(''x<sub>i</sub>''). See {{section link|Filters in topology#Tychonoff's theorem}} for the ingredients used here.

In the above proof, the axiom of choice is used two times: (1) to construct ultrafilters to characterize compactness and (2) to pick limit points <math>x_i</math>. Conversely, Tychonoff's theorem implies the axiom of choice; see {{section link||Proof of the axiom of choice from Tychonoff's theorem}} below. Thus, the use of the axiom of choice in the proof is unavoidable in general. However, if each factor <math>X_i</math> is Hausdorff, each limit point <math>x_i</math> is unique and so the second use of Choice is unnecessary. Ultrafilters, on the other hand, can be constructed by the [[Boolean prime ideal theorem]] or BPI (in the form of [[ultrafilter lemma]]) and, conversely, the Hausdorff version of the theorem implies BPI; see the remark at the end of {{section link||Application: the Hahn–Banach theorem}}. (Studying the ''strength'' of Tychonoff's theorem for various restricted classes of spaces is a topic in [[set-theoretic topology]].)

3)' Adapting the above proof, it is also possible to give a proof directly from [[Zorn's lemma]]; see {{section link|Zorn's_lemma|A proof of Tychonoff's theorem}}. (For example, in his textbook, [[James Munkres|Munkres]] gives such a proof.)

4) Similarly, the [[Moore-Smith sequence|Moore–Smith]] theory of convergence via nets, as supplemented by Kelley's notion of a [[Net (mathematics)|universal net]], leads to the criterion that a space is compact if and only if each universal net on the space converges. This criterion leads to a proof <ref>{{Citation |last=Kelley |first=John L. |title=Convergence in topology |journal=[[Duke Mathematical Journal]] |volume=17 |issue=3 |pages=277–283 |year=1950 |doi=10.1215/S0012-7094-50-01726-1 }}.
</ref> of Tychonoff's theorem, which is, word for word, identical to the Cartan/Bourbaki proof using filters, save for the repeated substitution of "universal net" for "ultrafilter". A proof using nets but not universal nets was given in 1992 by Paul Chernoff; see just below.

5) For compact Hausdorff spaces, the theorem (a product of compact Hausdorff spaces is compact Hausdorff) can be deduced from a corresponding result for locales: namely, a product of [[compact locale]]s is compact.<ref>{{harvnb|Johnstone|1982|loc=Ch. III., § 1.10.}}</ref>

=== Proof using nets ===
A proof here,<ref>Theorem 4.42. in {{cite book |last1=Folland |first1=Gerald B. |authorlink=Gerald Folland |title=Real Analysis: Modern Techniques and Their Applications |date=2007 |publisher=Wiley |edition=2nd}}</ref> due to P. Chernoff, is based on the following characterization of compactness in terms of nets:
*A space is compact if and only if each net on it has a cluster point.

Given a family of compact sets <math>X_a</math> indexed by a set <math>A</math>, to show
:<math>\prod_{a \in A} X_a</math>
is compact, we can therefore show each net <math>\langle x_{\alpha} \mid \alpha \in I \rangle</math> on it has a cluster point.

We shall identity the product <math>\prod_{a \in A} X_a</math> as thet set of all maps <math>f : A \to \cup_{a \in A} X_a</math> such that <math>f(a) \in X_a</math>; in fact, this is the usual definition of a set-theoretic product. Then finding a required cluster point amounts to constructing such a map with the required property. For that, consider the set
:<math>E := \{ f : B \to Y \mid B \subset A, f(b) \in X_b, \, f \, \text{ a cluster point of } \, {x_i}|_B \}</math>
where <math>Y = \cup_{a \in A} X_a</math>. We give this set the ordering by restriction; i.e., <math>f \le g</math> if and only if <math>f</math> is the restriction of <math>g</math>.

We now claim the hypothesis of Zorn's lemma is satisfied. For that, let <math>f_i : B_i \to Y</math> be a chain in the above <math>E</math> and define <math>f : B \to Y</math> by <math>B = \cup_i B_i</math> and <math>f|_{B_i} = f_i</math>. To show <math>f</math> is a cluster point of <math>{x_i}|_B</math>, let <math>U</math> be a basic neighborhood of <math>f</math> in <math>\prod_{a \in B} X_a.</math> By definition, it can be written as <math>U = \prod_{c \in C} U_c \times \prod_{b \in B - C} X_b</math> for some finite subset <math>C \subset B</math> and open subsets <math>U_c \subset X_c</math>. Now, since <math>C</math> is finite, <math>C \subset B_i</math> for large enough <math>i</math>. And since <math>f|_{B_i}</math> is a cluster point of the net <math>x_{\alpha}|_{B_i}</math>, for each <math>\alpha \in I</math>, we can find a <math>\beta \ge \alpha</math> such that <math>x_{\beta}|_{B_i} \in \prod_{c \in C} U_c \times \prod_{b \in B_i - C} X_b</math> and thus <math>x_{\beta}|_{B} \in U</math> as required.

Hence, by Zorn's lemma, we can find a maximal element <math>f : B \to Y</math> in <math>E</math>. We shall show <math>B = A</math>. Suppose otherwise; then there is an element <math>a \in A - B</math>. Now, <math>f|_{B}</math> is a cluster point of <math>\langle x_{\alpha}|_B \mid \alpha \in I \rangle</math> and so we can find a subnet <math>x' : J \to I \overset{x}\to \prod X_a</math> of the net <math>x</math> such that <math>x'_{\alpha}|_{B}</math> converges to <math>f|_B</math>. Since <math>X_a</math> is compact, <math>x'_{\alpha}|_{\{a\}}</math> has a cluster point, and so similarly we can find a subnet <math>x''</math> of <math>x'</math> that converges on <math>\{ a \}</math>, to some point of <math>X_a</math>. Thus, we can extend <math>f</math> to <math>g</math> that is a limit of <math>x''|_{B \cup \{a\}}</math>, a contradiction to the maximality of <math>f</math>. <math>\square</math>

=== Proof of the axiom of choice from Tychonoff's theorem ===

To prove that Tychonoff's theorem in its general version implies the axiom of choice, we establish that every infinite [[cartesian product]] of non-empty sets is nonempty. The trickiest part of the proof is introducing the right topology. The right topology, as it turns out, is the [[cofinite topology]] with a small twist. It turns out that every set given this topology automatically becomes a compact space. Once we have this fact, Tychonoff's theorem can be applied; we then use the [[finite intersection property]] (FIP) definition of compactness. The proof itself (due to [[J. L. Kelley]]) follows:<ref>{{Citation |last=Johnstone |first=Peter T. |title=Tychonoff's theorem without the axiom of choice |journal=[[Fundamenta Mathematicae]] |volume=113 |pages=21–35 |year=1981 |doi=10.4064/fm-113-1-21-35|doi-access=free }}.</ref>

Let {''A<sub>i</sub>''} be an indexed family of nonempty sets, for ''i'' ranging in ''I'' (where ''I'' is an arbitrary indexing set). We wish to show that the cartesian product of these sets is nonempty. Now, for each ''i'', take ''X<sub>i</sub>'' to be ''A<sub>i</sub>'' with the index ''i'' itself tacked on (renaming the indices using the [[disjoint union]] if necessary, we may assume that ''i'' is not a member of ''A<sub>i</sub>'', so simply take ''X<sub>i</sub>'' = ''A<sub>i</sub>'' ∪ {''i''}).

Now define the cartesian product
<math display=block>X = \prod_{i \in I} X_i</math>
along with the natural projection maps ''π<sub>i</sub>'' which take a member of ''X'' to its ''i''th term.

We give each ''X<sub>j</sub>'' the topology whose open sets are: the empty set, the singleton {''i''}, the set ''X<sub>i</sub>''. This makes ''X<sub>i</sub>'' compact, and by Tychonoff's theorem, ''X'' is also compact (in the product topology). The projection maps are continuous; all the ''A<sub>i</sub>'''s are closed, being complements of the [[singleton (mathematics)|singleton]] open set {''i''} in ''X<sub>i</sub>''. So the inverse images π<sub>''i''</sub><sup>−1</sup>(''A<sub>i</sub>'') are closed subsets of ''X''. We note that
<math display=block>\prod_{i \in I} A_i = \bigcap_{i \in I} \pi_i^{-1}(A_i) </math>
and prove that these inverse images have the FIP. Let ''i<sub>1</sub>'', ..., ''i<sub>N</sub>'' be a finite collection of indices in ''I''. Then the ''finite'' product ''A<sub>i<sub>1</sub></sub>'' × ... × ''A<sub>i<sub>N</sub></sub>''
is non-empty (only finitely many choices here, so AC is not needed); it merely consists of ''N''-tuples. Let  ''a'' = (''a''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''a<sub>N</sub>'') be such an ''N''-tuple. We extend ''a'' to the whole index set: take ''a'' to the function ''f'' defined by ''f''(''j'') = ''a<sub>k</sub>'' if ''j'' = ''i<sub>k</sub>'', and ''f''(''j'') = ''j'' otherwise. ''This step is where the addition of the extra point to each space is crucial'', for it allows us to define ''f'' for everything outside of the ''N''-tuple in a precise way without choices (we can already choose, by construction, ''j'' from ''X<sub>j</sub>'' ). π''<sub>i<sub>k</sub></sub>''(''f'') = ''a<sub>k</sub>'' is obviously an element of each ''A<sub>i<sub>k</sub></sub>'' so that ''f'' is in each inverse image; thus we have
<math display=block>\bigcap_{k = 1}^N \pi_{i_k}^{-1}(A_{i_k}) \neq \varnothing.</math>

By the FIP definition of compactness, the entire intersection over ''I'' must be nonempty, and the proof is complete.

== Application: the Hahn–Banach theorem ==
A standard proof of the [[Hahn-Banach theorem]] in functional analysis uses the axiom of choice in the form of [[Zorn's lemma]]. Tychonoff's theorem for compact Hausdorff spaces, which is strictly weaker than the axiom of choice and is equivalent to the [[Boolean prime ideal theorem]],<ref>Theorem 3.4. in https://dml.cz/bitstream/handle/10338.dmlcz/118951/CommentatMathUnivCarolRetro_38-1997-3_10.pdf</ref> can be used to give an alternative proof.<ref>Łoś, J. and Ryll-Nardzewski, C. (1951) On the application of Tychonoﬀ’s theorem in mathematical proofs, Fund. Math. 38, 233–237.</ref>

Specifically, Tychonoff's theorem in the Hausdorff case is used to deduce the following variant of the axiom of choice. Given a family of nonempty compact Hausdorff spaces <math>K_x, \, x \in X</math> parametrized by a set <math>X</math>, by a ''choice function'' for it, we shall mean a function
:<math>c : X \to U := \cup_{x \in X} K_x</math>
such that <math>c(x) \in K_x</math> for each <math>x</math>. Also, for a relation <math>R</math> on <math>U</math>; i.e., a subset of <math>U \times U</math>, we say such <math>c</math> is ''<math>R</math>-consistent on a set <math>S \subset X</math>'' if <math>(c(x), c(y)) \in R</math> for each <math>x, y \in S</math>.

{{math_theorem|name=Lemma|Assume, for each <math>x, y</math> in <math>X</math>, that <math>R \cap (K_x \times K_y)</math> is closed. Also, assume that for each finite subset <math>S \subset X</math>, there is a choice function for the family <math>K_x, \, x \in X</math> that is <math>R</math>-consistent on <math>S</math>.

Then there exists a choice function for the family <math>K_x</math> that is <math>R</math>-consistent on <math>X</math>.}}

''Proof of lemma'': let <math>P = \prod_{x \in X} K_x</math>, which is nonempty<ref>The nonempty-ness is a part of Tychonoff's theorem for compact Hausdorff spaces.</ref> and compact (also Hausdorff). Consider the family <math>P^S</math> parametrized by finite subsets <math>S \subset X</math> and given by
:<math>P^S =</math> the set of all <math>c \in P</math> that are <math>R</math>-consistent on <math>S</math>.
Each <math>P^S</math> is the intersection of <math>p_{x, y}^{-1}(R \cap (K_x \times K_y))</math> over <math>x, y \in S</math>, where <math>p_{x, y}(c) = (p_x(c), p_y(c))</math>. Thus, it is closed and nonempty by assumption. By compactness, the intersection <math>\cap_S P^S</math> is nonempty and any element of it (which we can pick without the axiom of choice) is a required choice function. <math>\square</math>

Now, the Hahn-Banach theorem is proved as follows. Given a linear functional <math>f</math> on a subspace <math>V_0 \subset V</math> dominated by a seminorm <math>p</math>, consider
*<math>X</math> = the set of all finite-dimensional subspaces of <math>V</math>.
*For each <math>W \in X</math>, <math>W'</math> = its dual and <math>K_W = \{ g \in W' \mid g|_{W \cap V_0} = f|_{W \cap V_0}, \, |g| \le p \}.</math>
*<math>R = \{ (g, h) \in K_{W_1} \times K_{W_2} \mid W_i \in X, \, g|_{W_1 \cap W_2} = h|_{W_1 \cap W_2} \}</math>.
It is easy to see the assumptions of the lemma are satisfied and thus we find an <math>R</math>-consistent choice function <math>c</math>. Then the functional <math>g(x) = c(W)(x), \, W = \operatorname{span} \{ x \}</math> is a required extension.

Incidentally, essentially the same proof can show that Tychonoff's theorem for compact Hausdorff spaces implies the Boolean prime ideal theorem.<ref>Łoś, J. and Ryll-Nardzewski, C., 1955. Effectiveness of the representation theory for Boolean algebras. Fundamenta Mathematicae, 41(1), pp.49-56.</ref> Indeed, on a Boolean algebra <math>B</math>, like in ring theory, to give a prime ideal is to give a homomorphism <math>B \to 2</math>. Then the idea in the above proof can be used to construct such a homomorphism, finishing the proof.
